text: Relojes Centenario, the first manufacturer of monumental clocks in Latin America, was founded by Alberto Olvera Hernández in the municipality of Zacatlán, Puebla, Mexico, as a workshop on his family farm when he was a teenager. His first clock served the family farm, and the next was installed in the main church of Chignahuapan in 1919, a project that took a year to complete and remains operational to this day. In 1921, the company adopted the name Relojes Centenario to commemorate the centennial of the end of the Mexican War of Independence. Olvera Hernández, born on March 2, 1892, at the Coyotepec farm outside Zacatlán, demonstrated early mechanical aptitude, receiving a patent in 1920 for a track changer for electric trains, and developed an interest in clocks after repairing a broken clock on his home’s chimney. In 1912, at 17 years old, he built his first monumental clock using scrap and wood from the farm, and by 1929, the business had grown to include a helper and apprentices. He moved his workshop to Zacatlán to establish Relojes Centenario, which remains in the same location. From 1918 to the present, the company has manufactured over 2,000 monumental clocks for churches, government buildings, towers, shopping centers, hotels, and other sites, and has restored and automated more than 600 European-origin clocks. They also service clocks across Mexico and train local workers in their maintenance. The next clock after Chignahuapan was installed in Libres in 1921. In 1930, Olvera Hernández founded La Quinta María as a second workshop, and in 1966, the company acquired its current central location in Zacatlán, enabling increased production. In 1975, the business became a legal corporation. The company is currently managed by the sons and grandsons of Olvera Hernández, with José Luis Olvera Charolet serving as general manager. Each year, they install between seventy and eighty clocks in Mexico and abroad, with over 1,500 Centenario clocks in Mexico alone. In 1982, the company opened an office in Mexico City at Colonia Tepeyac Insurgentes. In 1986, it constructed a floral clock in Zacatlán’s main square, which features two faces, five meters in diameter, controlled by a single mechanism, and includes nine mechanical carillons that play nine different melodies depending on the time of year and day, chiming at 6am, 10am, 2pm, and 9pm to avoid conflicting with mass hours. This clock is the first of its kind and has become a symbol of the town. In 1993, the Museo de Relojería Alberto Olvera Hernández was opened in the upper level of the factory, named after the founder, and is free to the public. The gift shop, “La Casa del Tiempo,” opened in 2003. In the 2000s, the company introduced digital chimes programmed for funeral songs and “Ave Maria.” Each clock is unique, with no two being exactly alike. Notable clocks include a large floral clock in Mexico City’s Parque Hundido, covering 78 m² with a ten-meter-wide face, and a clock in the Nuestra Señora del Roble basilica in Monterrey with four four-meter faces. The Tulantepec clock chimes the national anthem and “Himno Guadalupano” at 6am and 6pm, with quarter-hour chimes and is fully automated using counterweights. Clocks in Torreón play “La Filomena” hourly, in Tuxtla Gutiérrez the Tuxtla waltz and “La Chiapanecas,” and in Santa Bárbara, Chihuahua, “Amor Perdido” is played. The company also repairs German and French clocks installed in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The museum contains replicas and original timepieces illustrating the history of timekeeping, including sundials from 2000 BCE, candle clocks with oil lamps, and mechanical clocks. A unique exhibit is a statue of Merlin, whose arms indicate time only for twelve hours, resting at night. Visitors can walk through the factory to access the museum, where they can observe the entire process from metal smelting to final testing. A stairwell connects the museum to the factory floor and features a mural depicting key events in Olvera Hernández’s life, including his central position in a ring of icons related to time, books on his self-education, a portrait of his wife Maria Charolet, twelve figures representing his children, and the violin and mandolin he played.
